## Testing stock assessments against a simulated ecosystem: an Atlantis-to-CEATTLE framework for Gulf of Alaska groundfish

.pull-left-40[
.table[
**Goal:** evaluate how projected scenarios may challenge Gulf of Alaska stock assessment models under non-stationarity

**Operating model (Atlantis):** simulates populations under projected climate and fishing scenarios

**Data (<span style="color: cornflowerblue;">atlantisom</span>):** simulated sampling of Atlantis mimics surveys and fisheries, including survey precision, sample sizes ([`atlantisom`](https://github.com/r4atlantis/atlantisom))

**Assessment model (<span style="color: darkorange;">CEATTLE</span>):** fit to the simulated data; estimates are compared against the known truth

**Proof of concept:** GOA walleye pollock; survey design and model structure mimic the operational assessment

**Findings:** assessment complexity must match Atlantis, which is a simplification of reality; misspecifications of natural mortality and fishery selectivity introduce bias
]
.footnote[Slide courtesy Alberto Rovellini <arovel@uw.edu>]
]

.pull-right-60[]

???
Figure:
Proof of concept example of the workflow:

Atlantis run for 100 years (1990-2090). Noise in pollock biomass generated by forcing rec devs, randomly sampled from assessment estimates

Atlantisom used to generate survey index, catch time series, survey and fisher length and age compositions. Data structure mimics that of the GOA pollock assessment (two survey indices, age compositions, selectivity to match, etc.).

Fits are preliminary but highlight where the model introduces bias compared to the truth from Atlantis. Using a set of model diagnostics (e.g., retrospective analyses, bottom right panel) to evaluate model fits and identify potential nonstationary dynamics.

Next steps: refine pollock, extend to single-species pacific cod and arrowtooth flounder, set up multispecies runs with the three species (as done in the ESR)

Run more Atlantis scenarios (climate, production, recruitment, fishing strategies, etc), repeat fits, evaluate emerging bias.

## Model-derived scenarios of forage fish productivity and distribution for management strategy evaluation

### How to integrate climate uncertainty into MSE

Defining future state of nature by generating range of operating models (OMs): Approach depends on understanding of climate and biology/fisheries relationship and availability of oceanographic projections

<span style="color: cornflowerblue;">EMPIRICAL APPROACH</span> (sensu [Punt et al. 2014](https://doi.org/10.1093/icesjms/fst057)) - Consult experts to define potential scenarios, no direct climate-biology/fisheries link identified. Easily implementable but hard to assign plausibility 

.footnote[Figure from [Siple et al. 2021](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/faf.12579)]

???
WGSAM: This work summarizes a manuscript in review, led by Dr. Desiree Tommasi from UC Santa Cruz/  NOAA SWFSC.  This is relevant to TOR E (MSE), among other TORs. 
The title is: Model-derived scenarios of forage fish productivity and distribution for management strategy evaluation
MSEs can simulate potential, but uncertain, effects of climate change on the biological and fisheries system – [Walters et al. 2023](https://doi.org/10.1093/icesjms/fsad031)

background-size: 1000px

## How to integrate climate uncertainty into MSE

<span style="color: cornflowerblue;">MECHANISTIC APPROACH</span> (sensu [Punt et al. 2014](https://doi.org/10.1093/icesjms/fst057)) - Use climate-informed OM. 

If complex ecosystem model, high computational needs. 

If climate-enhanced single species model, statistical relationship between environment and vital rates may break down

.footnote[Figure from [de Moor et al. 2023](https://doi.org/10.1139/cjfas-2023-0092)]

---
background-image: url("https://github.com/sgaichas/HSpresentations/raw/main/docs/images/DesireeWCoastWGSAM2026_3.png")
background-size: 1000px
background-position: bottom

## How to integrate climate uncertainty into MSE

<span style="color: cornflowerblue;">HYBRID APPROACH</span> (this study) 

Use existing climate-informed ecosystem models to develop climate-informed uncertainty scenarios for OM parameters. 

Less computationally intensive to run than mechanistic approach, but still process-based 

.footnote[Figure from [Siple et al. 2021](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/faf.12579)]

---

background-size: 1000px
background-position: bottom

## Application to Pacific Sardine Northern Subpopulation

*  Leverages existing projections of vital rates and distribution for the northern subpopulation of Pacific sardine from regional ecological models to develop quantitative scenarios for MSE-like closed-loop simulations 
*  Ecological model output informs recruitment, growth, natural mortality, or catchability parameters in MSE OMs 
*  OMs based on single species OM similar to stock assessment ([Wildermuth et al. 2024](https://doi.org/10.1139/cjfas-2023-0169)) 
*  Ecological models used are DynaMICE ([Koenigstein et al. 2022](https://doi.org/10.1093/icesjms/fsac191)), the end-to-end Atlantis ecosystem model ([Liu et al. 2025](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1111/gcb.70021)), an Individual Based Model (IBM, [Fiechter et al. 2021](https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2021.685241)), and Species Distribution Models (SDMs, [Muhling et al. 2025](https://doi.org/10.1111/fog.12730)) 
*  Climate projections from three global Earth System Models (ESMs) and emission scenario RCP 8.5, downscaled for U.S. West Coast using a regional ocean model ([Pozo-Buil et al. 2021](https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2021.612874)), were integrated into the ecological models

## Catchability scenario for MSE 
![Catchability](https://github.com/sgaichas/HSpresentations/raw/main/docs/images/DesireeWCoastWGSAM2026_5.png)
*  Catchability index is the proportion of the total probability of occurrence that is in the survey region 
*  5.48% to 13.4% decrease in future catchability relative to historical (2001-2020) depending on the time block 

]

???
WGSAM: as an example,   future changes in catchability are incorporated into the OM, informed by detailed SDMs.  The SDMs here represent the distribution of sardine larvae. Covariates considered in the SDM  included SST, isothermal layer depth, buoyancy frequency, and total kinetic energy, as well as surface chlorophyll, spatial standard deviation of SST, moon phase, and distance to nearest land .  These SDMs are projected under different forcings from the GFDL, Hadley, and IPSL earth system models. Generally, they predict a northward shift of the stock under climate change. Hypothetically, a survey only in the south would experience decreasing catchability in the coming decades. 

Based on these SDMs, Hypothetically, a survey only in the south would experience decreasing catchability in the coming decades.  This can be included within the OM. 
 


---
## Conclusions: Hybrid approach of Using Ecological Models to Drive Climate-informed MSE scenarios

*  Enhanced ecological realism as compared to empirical MSE scenarios approaches 
*  Less computing intensive than using a process-based model as OM, enabling larger exploration of uncertainty space 
*  Integration of output of ecological models into simpler single-species OM necessitates a rescaling process to address the mismatch in ecological resolution 
*  Pacific sardine vital rates highly variable, climate driven change in parameter small relative to interannual variability 
*  Ecological model output is useful for generating MSE scenarios beyond changes directly driven by climate (e.g. density dependent predation mortality from Atlantis ecosystem model) 

<span style="color: blue;">Scenarios for recruitment, growth, M, and catchability have now been incorporated into OM, for projections to year 2068 under 2 Earth System Model forcings

.center[Thanks to the [Future Seas](https://joshcullen.github.io/Future_Seas_Website/) [Team](https://joshcullen.github.io/Future_Seas_Website/Team/)]

.footnote[Slides courtesy Desiree Tommasi, <detommas@ucsc.edu> and Isaac Kaplan, <isaac.kaplan@noaa.gov>]

???
The manuscript is currently in NOAA internal review, and will be submitted to CJFAS.

## Northeast US ecosystem and habitat indicators in assessment and management

.pull-left-70[
[Advection index](https://noaa-edab.github.io/catalog/advection.html#advection)
Intent: a proxy for larval retention, inform recruitment prediction
Data: HYbrid Coordinate Ocean Model (HYCOM, hycom.org)

<br /><br /><br /><br /><br /><br /><br /><br />

*  Advection Indices: cross-transect velocity calculated along shelf edge (negative velocity = offshore advection). 
*  Velocities summed across depths for 3 depth ranges and averaged monthly March-June for 2 regions to match species spawning strategies. 
*  Expect lower larval retention and survival of recruits in regions/ years/months/depths of high off-shelf advection  

.footnote[Slide courtesy Laurel Smith <laurel.smith@noaa.gov>]

]

.pull-right-30[]


???
•In middle plot, red arrows are New England and blue arrows are mid-Atlantic regions
•Right panel: Months are labeled at the top bar of plots
•Mid-Atlantic shows long-term trends of increasing offshore advection in shallow and deepest depth ranges in June
•New England shows long-term trends of increasing onshore advection in mid and deepest depth ranges in June
•New England shows short-term trend of increasing offshore advection in the mid depth range in March
•These trends can be paired with species that spawn and disperse larvae in specific regions, months and depths
•Could be added to Risk Framework for management

## Northeast US ecosystem and habitat indicators in assessment and management

### Predation Pressure Index

A simple anomaly around an assumed natural mortality ($M_b$=0.2)
Based on the sum of predator ($j$) biomass changes over time ($B_{i,j}$) and a static percent frequency of occurrence of mackerel in the diet ($P_j$), averaged over the time series:
.pull-left-30[

$$PPI_i = \sum_j \left( B_{i,j} * P_j \right )$$

Time varying natural
 mortality:

$$M_i = \frac{M_b * PPI_i}{\overline{PPI}}$$

Added a daily per capita consumption per body mass scalar to make predator groups comparable  
Ensured appropriate spatial-temporal overlap
]

.pull-right-70[
.table[
Predation pressure for each group separately.  &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; **Time varying M** combining all pred groups
]
]

.footnote[Slide courtesy Laurel Smith <laurel.smith@noaa.gov>]


???
PPI is based on Richards and Jacobson (2016) paper
Natural mortality is currently assumed to be 0.2 for mackerel assessment
PPI would vary Mi around assumed M based on predation pressure
We added a DCC scalar since predator species had order of magnitude different metabolic rates
Plot on left shows predation pressures of individual predators (following biomass trends over time)
Plot on the right is sequentially adding predators to get a Mi for all combined predators (black line)

## Priority Decision 2: Catch/Quota Setting

.table[
.ltbluebox[
**1. Determine Assessment Priorities**  
The NRCC prioritizes stocks for assessment based on management needs,
fishery importance, stock status and trend, ecosystem importance, assessment information, and stock
biology. Terms of Reference (ToRs) ensure the assessment process delivers consistent, management-relevant outputs.
]

.ltbluebox[
**2. Conduct Assessment**  
Assessment scientists assemble and analyze fishery dependent and independent data and develop models to synthesize the data and produce outputs meeting the assessment ToRs. 
]

.ltpurplebox[
**3. Review Assessment**  
Independent reviewers evaluate whether assessments ToRs are met, data is appropriate, and methods reflect best practices.
]
]
]

.pull-right[
.table[
.ltgreenbox[
### Council Steps 

.ltbluebox[
**4. Determine Acceptable Biological Catch (ABC)**  
The SSC uses reviewed assessment outputs within a structured framework to determine ABC from assessment uncertainty based on input data, model diagnostics and performance, and ecosystem considerations.
]

.ltbluebox[
**5. Catch Limits, Targets, and Quotas**  
The Council decides whether annually varying or averaged ABCs will be used in multiyear harvest specifications, then allocates the ABC to harvest sectors. Management uncertainty is determined and applied, then discards are estimated and subtracted to derive quotas and harvest limits.
]
]
]

Indicators could be used at any step but 3. 
Indicators are already used in Assessments and in SSC ABC Determinations.
]





---
## A potential framework

### Identify the decision

Risk policy: Council decides whether to apply the standard biology-based risk policy, or modify with social and economic factors? How much weight should social and economic factors get?

Catch/quota setting: SSC decides on assessment level, then decides on either OFL CV level using the structured process, or decides on an ABC

Catch/quota setting: Monitoring Committee decides whether to apply management uncertainty buffers to establish annual catch targets to account for inability to manage the catch or uncertainty in catch estimates

Catch/quota setting: Monitoring Committee decides how to estimate (dead) discards to set quotas or harvest limits

### Identify key information 

Which are the most important two factors to consider for the decision? Combined socioeconomic and biological?

What indicators do we have for the factors?

### Identify clear decision criteria

What threshold values move us between decisions?

# Brainstorm: Indicator use in SSC ABC decisions

## Clarify Current OFL CV Process 
*  Include more CVA indicators under the ecosystem criterion (potential for distribution shift, directional effect)
*  Develop a rubric to integrate standard indicators into a single ecosystem OFL CV rank 
*  Consider ecosystem indicators under data quality or assessment performance 

--

.pull-left[
## Modify Current OFL CV Process 
*  Develop indicator thresholds where ecosystem factors have higher weight   
*  Expand ecosystem factors to include Pacific categories:
    +  Food webs
    +  Habitat availability
    +  Changes in ecosystem productivity
    +  Physiological indices
    +  Reproductive indices
]

--

.pull-right[
## New Processes 
*  Use ecosystem information to modify ABC when there is no OFL
*  Use ecosystem information to adjust short term projections
*  Use ecosystem information to decide when to devaite from previously specified ABC
